title: "Spatial Classifier"
date: 2026-09-11
categories: [tool, geoml]
description: "Turn field samples of a category (soil type, habitat, land use, anything recorded as a class at scattered points) into a map of the likely class everywhere in the area, with a Random Forest trained on location, see where that map is confident and where it's guessing, and score it with spatial block cross-validation instead of a flattering random split. Runs entirely in your browser, powered by Python."
page-layout: full
---

You recorded a category at scattered points: soil type at sampling
pits, habitat at survey plots, land use at field checks. This tool
maps the **likely class everywhere in between**, shows how sure it is
about each part of that map, and scores it on whole areas it wasn't
trained on, not just on scattered points next to ones it was.

Upload a point file with a column that labels each point's class
(`.geojson`, or a shapefile as a single `.zip` or as
`.shp`/`.dbf`/`.shx` selected together), pick that column, and a
Random Forest learns which class tends to occur where. The model uses
**only each point's position**, not the file's other columns: it
answers "given what was found nearby, what's probably here?" It's the
categorical counterpart of the
[Kriging Interpolator](/tools/kriging-interpolator.html), which does
the same for a numeric value like pH or moisture.

::: {.callout-tip}
**Private by design.** Your file is processed entirely in your
browser (Python via WebAssembly) — it's never uploaded to any server,
including ours. Nothing to configure, nothing to trust: the code
never gets the chance to see your data.
:::

```{.webgeods-python #spatial-classifier-example-py}
import json

# Deterministic synthetic survey, the same one the companion article
# (Predicting Spatial Classes with Random Forest) builds from the same
# rule: 30 survey sites, 5 points recorded close together at each,
# three bands whose boundaries undulate across the area, and one site
# in five sitting on a local patch of a different class.
#
# Sampled in SITES on purpose, because that's how field surveys are
# usually collected and it's what makes the validation choice matter.
# An earlier version put the points on an even lattice with
# independent label noise, one point in nine flipped on its own. On
# that layout random and spatial-block validation scored the same
# (measured: 5-fold CV 0.61-0.63 vs 0.57-0.67), so the Held out
# selector had nothing to show. Here a random holdout keeps each test
# point's site-mates in training, and the patches make those
# site-mates informative in a way the model can't know from anywhere
# else: measured live, 5-fold CV 0.76 random vs 0.57 in blocks.
NEXT_CLASS = {"south": "centre", "centre": "north", "north": "south"}
SITE_OFFSETS = [(0, 0), (1, 0.4), (-0.6, 0.9), (-0.8, -0.7), (0.5, -1)]

features = []
for s in range(30):
    col, row = s % 6, s // 6
    cx = (col + 0.5) / 6 + ((s * 37) % 11 - 5) / 110
    cy = (row + 0.5) / 5 + ((s * 53) % 13 - 6) / 130
    for k, (dx, dy) in enumerate(SITE_OFFSETS):
        x, y = cx + dx * 0.02, cy + dy * 0.02
        # Triangular wave along x: the band boundaries rise and fall,
        # so no single horizontal cut separates the classes.
        u, v = x * 15, y * 10
        tri = abs((2 * u) % 8 - 4) - 2
        cls = "south" if v < 3 + tri else ("centre" if v < 6 + tri else "north")
        if s % 5 == 2:
            cls = NEXT_CLASS[cls]
        features.append({
            "type": "Feature",
            "properties": {"name": f"site {s + 1} point {k + 1}", "class": cls},
            "geometry": {"type": "Point", "coordinates": [12.4450 + x * 0.0150, 41.8850 + y * 0.0120]}
        })

with open("/uploaded.geojson", "w") as f:
    json.dump({"type": "FeatureCollection", "features": features}, f)

{"written": "/uploaded.geojson", "points": len(features)}
```

```{.webgeods-python #spatial-classifier-inspect-py}
#| package: geopandas
import geopandas as gpd

def export_crs(g):
    # Reprojects `g` back to the CRS it was UPLOADED in (original_crs,
    # set below and reused as a module-level global by the compute
    # cell) -- every downloadable result goes through this, even
    # though the map/classification above always work in WGS84
    # (GeoJSON and MapLibre both assume it). Same pattern as this
    # project's other vector tools (e.g. the Validator, the clustering
    # explorer).
    if g is None or original_crs is None or str(original_crs) == "EPSG:4326":
        return g
    return g.to_crs(original_crs)

EMPTY_FC = {"type": "FeatureCollection", "features": []}

# No built-in fallback: if nothing is readable, gdf stays None and the
# result is an empty FeatureCollection -- this cell only ever runs
# after a successful upload or "Load example".
gdf = None
for path in ["/uploaded.geojson", "/uploaded.shp", "/vsizip//uploaded.zip"]:
    try:
        gdf = gpd.read_file(path)
        break
    except Exception:
        pass

crs_warning = None
original_crs = None
summary_out = None
if gdf is not None:
    if gdf.crs is None:
        gdf = gdf.set_crs("EPSG:4326")
        crs_warning = "No CRS found in the uploaded file — assuming WGS84 (EPSG:4326)."
    original_crs = gdf.crs
    if str(original_crs) != "EPSG:4326":
        gdf = gdf.to_crs("EPSG:4326")

    columns = [c for c in gdf.columns if c != "geometry"]
    summary_out = {
        "count": int(len(gdf)),
        "crs": str(original_crs),
        "columns": columns
    }

{
    "features": gdf.__geo_interface__ if gdf is not None else EMPTY_FC,
    "crsWarning": crs_warning,
    "summary": summary_out
}
```

The code itself isn't shown here — it's a fixed, non-editable
computation using scikit-learn's `RandomForestClassifier` underneath.
Want to see it built up step by step, in Python *and* R — including a
real gotcha where the two languages disagree on classification vs.
regression? Read
[Predicting Spatial Classes with Random Forest](/posts/spatial-classification.html).

```{.webgeods-python #spatial-classifier-compute-py}
#| inject: [classColumn, holdout, nTrees, gridResolution]
#| package: geopandas, scikit-learn
import warnings
import numpy as np
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier
from sklearn.model_selection import KFold, StratifiedKFold, train_test_split
from sklearn.neighbors import NearestNeighbors
from shapely.geometry import Polygon, box

# Reuses the WGS84 `gdf` already read and CRS-normalized by the
# inspect cell above (same session -- same pattern as the clustering
# explorer's compute cell reusing its own inspect cell's `gdf`),
# rather than re-reading the file.
labeled = gdf[gdf[classColumn].notna()].copy()
labeled[classColumn] = labeled[classColumn].astype(str)

# Working/calculation CRS: a Random Forest fit on raw degrees would
# treat 1 degree of longitude and 1 degree of latitude as the same
# "distance" everywhere on Earth, which they aren't -- same reasoning,
# same UTM auto-pick formula (bounding-box center, not a per-feature
# centroid mean), as this project's Buffer/Proximity and Spatial
# Clustering tools.
minx, miny, maxx, maxy = gdf.total_bounds
center_lon = float((minx + maxx) / 2)
center_lat = float((miny + maxy) / 2)
utm_zone = int((center_lon + 180) // 6) + 1
calc_epsg = 32600 + utm_zone if center_lat >= 0 else 32700 + utm_zone
calc_crs_label = f"EPSG:{calc_epsg}"

labeled_proj = labeled.to_crs(epsg=calc_epsg)
# .centroid, not .x/.y directly -- handles any geometry type uniformly
# (centroid of a point is the point itself), same defensive choice as
# this project's Spatial Clustering Explorer.
proj_x = labeled_proj.geometry.centroid.x.to_numpy()
proj_y = labeled_proj.geometry.centroid.y.to_numpy()

# A single UTM zone distorts badly -- to the point of returning inf --
# for points far enough from it (a real crash a global upload
# triggered: fitting on infinite coordinates fails deep inside
# scikit-learn with an opaque error). Drop those points here instead,
# with a clear message if too few remain, rather than letting that
# opaque error surface.
finite_mask = np.isfinite(proj_x) & np.isfinite(proj_y)
excluded_count = int((~finite_mask).sum())
labeled_proj = labeled_proj[finite_mask]
X = np.column_stack([proj_x[finite_mask], proj_y[finite_mask]])
y = labeled_proj[classColumn].values

if len(y) == 0:
    raise ValueError(
        f"None of the {len(labeled)} labeled points could be projected into "
        f"a single UTM zone ({calc_crs_label}) -- this dataset spans too wide "
        "an area for this tool's single-zone approach. Try a smaller, more "
        "local file."
    )

class_labels = sorted(set(y.tolist()))
if len(class_labels) < 2:
    raise ValueError(
        f"Only {len(class_labels)} distinct value(s) found in \"{classColumn}\" "
        "after projection -- need at least 2 classes to train a classifier."
    )
class_counts = {c: int((y == c).sum()) for c in class_labels}

# Spatial blocks: a fixed 4x4 grid over the labeled points' own extent,
# each block assigned to one of 5 folds by (bx + 2*by) % 5, a diagonal
# pattern that spreads every fold across the whole area instead of
# stacking it on one side. Deterministic on purpose (no random draw),
# so the same file always gets the same blocks, and the companion
# article's R tab gets exactly the same folds as its Python tab.
#
# Why blocks at all: points collected close together share local
# conditions the model can't see any other way. Hold out random points
# and a test point's neighbours usually stay in training, so the score
# measures "can it copy the point next door", not "can it predict a
# place it hasn't visited" -- the question a map is actually used for.
# 4x4 is a default, not a rule: a block should be wider than the
# distance over which samples resemble each other, which this tool
# can't know for an arbitrary upload.
BLOCKS_PER_SIDE = 4
N_FOLDS = 5
bminx, bminy = X.min(axis=0)
bmaxx, bmaxy = X.max(axis=0)
block_size = max(bmaxx - bminx, bmaxy - bminy, 1e-6) / BLOCKS_PER_SIDE
block_x = np.minimum(((X[:, 0] - bminx) // block_size).astype(int), BLOCKS_PER_SIDE - 1)
block_y = np.minimum(((X[:, 1] - bminy) // block_size).astype(int), BLOCKS_PER_SIDE - 1)
block_fold = (block_x + 2 * block_y) % N_FOLDS
use_blocks = holdout == "Spatial blocks"

# A class with exactly 1 member can never be held out for testing --
# there's no way to keep at least one example in training AND set one
# aside. Excluding just THOSE classes from the split (rather than
# vetoing it for the whole dataset the moment any single class is
# that small, the previous behavior) matters on real data: a long
# tail of rare categories is normal, and hundreds of well-populated
# points shouldn't lose their held-out accuracy because of one
# singleton elsewhere in the same column.
splittable_classes = {c for c in class_labels if class_counts[c] >= 2}
splittable_mask = np.isin(y, list(splittable_classes))
can_split = len(splittable_classes) >= 2 and int(splittable_mask.sum()) >= 6

# The split is done on ROW INDICES, not on the coordinate arrays
# directly: the confusion matrix below needs to say which individual
# points were held out and what each was predicted as, so that clicking
# a matrix cell can highlight exactly those points on the map. Splitting
# X/y alone would discard that identity.
splittable_idx = np.flatnonzero(splittable_mask)

# In blocks mode the held-out set is one whole fold of blocks -- the
# first one that leaves at least two classes and a handful of points to
# train on (fold 0 on any reasonably spread file). No stratification is
# possible here: a class can be missing from the held-out blocks
# entirely, and then simply has no per-class score, same as a
# singleton class in random mode.
test_fold = None
if use_blocks and len(y) >= 10:
    test_fold = next(
        (f for f in range(N_FOLDS)
         if (block_fold == f).any()
         and len(set(y[block_fold != f].tolist())) >= 2
         and int((block_fold != f).sum()) >= 5),
        None
    )
    can_split = test_fold is not None

if can_split and use_blocks:
    test_idx = np.flatnonzero(block_fold == test_fold)
    train_idx = np.flatnonzero(block_fold != test_fold)
    X_train, y_train = X[train_idx], y[train_idx]
    X_test, y_test = X[test_idx], y[test_idx]
elif can_split:
    train_idx, test_idx = train_test_split(
        splittable_idx, test_size=0.2, stratify=y[splittable_idx], random_state=0
    )
    # Singleton-class points never entered the split above -- always
    # trained on, never tested (there's nothing meaningful to test a
    # 1-example class against).
    train_idx = np.concatenate([train_idx, np.flatnonzero(~splittable_mask)])
    X_train, y_train = X[train_idx], y[train_idx]
    X_test, y_test = X[test_idx], y[test_idx]
else:
    train_idx = np.arange(len(y))
    test_idx = np.array([], dtype=int)
    X_train, y_train = X, y
    X_test, y_test = None, None

# Two forests, for two different jobs. eval_model never sees the
# held-out points: it's what the test accuracy, the confusion matrix
# and each held-out point's own prediction are measured on. The map
# comes from `model` below, trained on EVERY point, the usual practice:
# cross-validation scores the fitting procedure, not one particular
# fitted forest, so leaving points out of the final map would only
# make the map worse without making the score any truer. (An earlier
# version drew the map from eval_model, which in blocks mode meant
# mapping without the dashed blocks' points, exactly where it was
# being scored.)
eval_model = RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=int(nTrees), random_state=0)
eval_model.fit(X_train, y_train)

model = RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=int(nTrees), random_state=0)
model.fit(X, y)

accuracy = float((eval_model.predict(X_test) == y_test).mean()) if X_test is not None else None

# One held-out set is a single draw, and a noisy one: on the built-in
# example the held-out block fold alone scores 0.51 and the random
# 20% scores 0.87, both further apart than the 5-fold figures (0.57
# and 0.76) that average over every point. The comparison that actually
# answers "how much does a random holdout flatter this map" is 5-fold
# cross-validation under BOTH schemes, computed on every run whatever
# the selector says: every point is tested exactly once, by a model
# that never saw it. Costs 2 x 5 extra fits, negligible next to the
# grid prediction for the file sizes this tool is meant for.
def cv_accuracy(fold_ids):
    correct, total = 0, 0
    for f in np.unique(fold_ids):
        train_mask, test_mask = fold_ids != f, fold_ids == f
        if len(set(y[train_mask].tolist())) < 2:
            continue
        fold_model = RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=int(nTrees), random_state=0)
        fold_model.fit(X[train_mask], y[train_mask])
        correct += int((fold_model.predict(X[test_mask]) == y[test_mask]).sum())
        total += int(test_mask.sum())
    return correct / total if total else None

cv_random = cv_blocks = None
if len(y) >= 10:
    random_fold = np.empty(len(y), dtype=int)
    with warnings.catch_warnings():
        # StratifiedKFold warns (not fails) when a class has fewer than
        # 5 members; those points still get a fold, just not evenly.
        warnings.simplefilter("ignore")
        try:
            folds = StratifiedKFold(N_FOLDS, shuffle=True, random_state=0).split(X, y)
            for f, (_, fold_test) in enumerate(folds):
                random_fold[fold_test] = f
        except ValueError:
            # Every class smaller than 5: stratifying is impossible.
            for f, (_, fold_test) in enumerate(KFold(N_FOLDS, shuffle=True, random_state=0).split(X)):
                random_fold[fold_test] = f
    cv_random = cv_accuracy(random_fold)
    cv_blocks = cv_accuracy(block_fold)

# How far each scheme's test points sit from the nearest point the
# model trained on -- the thing that actually separates the two scores.
# A score only describes predictions made about as far from the data
# as its test points were, so the fair question is how that compares
# with the map's own cells (distance_map, set once the grid exists
# below). On the built-in example: random 27 m, blocks 193 m, map
# cells about 73 m. Random folds test closer to the data than the map
# ever predicts, so they flatter it; these blocks test further away,
# so they're on the cautious side. Measured separately (same points,
# UTM 33N), the block grids whose test distances best matched the
# map's (10x10, 12x12) scored 0.61-0.65, between the two figures
# shown; other grid sizes ranged 0.52-0.72, which is why this row
# reports distances rather than picking a block size automatically.
def nearest_distances(train_pts, query_pts):
    finder = NearestNeighbors(n_neighbors=1).fit(train_pts)
    return finder.kneighbors(query_pts)[0][:, 0]

def cv_test_distance(fold_ids):
    parts = [
        nearest_distances(X[fold_ids != f], X[fold_ids == f])
        for f in np.unique(fold_ids)
        if (fold_ids != f).any()
    ]
    return float(np.median(np.concatenate(parts))) if parts else None

distance_random = cv_test_distance(random_fold) if cv_random is not None else None
distance_blocks = cv_test_distance(block_fold) if cv_blocks is not None else None

# Per-class held-out accuracy -- feeds the second sidePanel chart
# (accuracy by class, next to the class-distribution chart): the
# overall accuracy above can hide a model that's perfect on the
# majority class and useless on a rare one. A class absent from
# class_accuracy (rather than 0.0) means "no held-out points for this
# class" -- a singleton-class point (see splittable_classes above), or
# no test split at all -- not "the model got it wrong every time",
# which 0.0 would misleadingly claim.
class_accuracy = {}
y_pred_test = None
if X_test is not None:
    y_pred_test = eval_model.predict(X_test)
    for c in class_labels:
        test_mask = y_test == c
        n = int(test_mask.sum())
        if n > 0:
            class_accuracy[c] = {
                "accuracy": float((y_pred_test[test_mask] == y_test[test_mask]).mean()),
                "testCount": n
            }

# Confusion matrix over the held-out points: which class was predicted
# for points that really belong to each class. The diagonal is the same
# information as class_accuracy above; the off-diagonal is what that
# number can't tell you -- WHERE the errors go.
#
# Only the pairs that actually occur are listed, not a full N x N grid:
# a file with many classes would otherwise carry a payload growing with
# the square of the class count, for a matrix that is mostly zeros. At
# most one entry per held-out point.
confusion = []
if y_pred_test is not None:
    pair_counts = {}
    for true_cls, pred_cls in zip(y_test.tolist(), y_pred_test.tolist()):
        pair_counts[(true_cls, pred_cls)] = pair_counts.get((true_cls, pred_cls), 0) + 1
    confusion = [
        {"trueClass": t, "predictedClass": p, "count": int(n)}
        for (t, p), n in sorted(pair_counts.items())
    ]

# Regular square-cell grid over the *full uploaded extent* (gdf's own
# bounds, not just the labeled subset) -- gridResolution cells along
# the longer side, square cells derived from that, capped in count by
# construction (gridResolution <= 40, so at most ~1600 cells)
# regardless of how large the uploaded extent is.
gdf_proj_full = gdf.to_crs(epsg=calc_epsg)
full_x = gdf_proj_full.geometry.centroid.x.to_numpy()
full_y = gdf_proj_full.geometry.centroid.y.to_numpy()
full_finite_mask = np.isfinite(full_x) & np.isfinite(full_y)
if not full_finite_mask.any():
    raise ValueError(
        f"None of the uploaded points could be projected into a single UTM "
        f"zone ({calc_crs_label}) -- this dataset spans too wide an area for "
        "this tool's single-zone approach. Try a smaller, more local file."
    )
# total_bounds() would propagate inf from any unprojectable point above --
# computed by hand here, over the finite subset only.
gminx, gmaxx = float(full_x[full_finite_mask].min()), float(full_x[full_finite_mask].max())
gminy, gmaxy = float(full_y[full_finite_mask].min()), float(full_y[full_finite_mask].max())
width, height = gmaxx - gminx, gmaxy - gminy
longer_side = max(width, height, 1e-6)
cell_size = longer_side / int(gridResolution)
n_cols = max(1, int(np.ceil(width / cell_size)))
n_rows = max(1, int(np.ceil(height / cell_size)))

centers_x, centers_y = [], []
for row in range(n_rows):
    for col in range(n_cols):
        centers_x.append(gminx + (col + 0.5) * cell_size)
        centers_y.append(gminy + (row + 0.5) * cell_size)
centers = np.column_stack([centers_x, centers_y])
predicted = model.predict(centers)
distance_map = float(np.median(nearest_distances(X, centers)))

# How much of the forest backs each cell's predicted class (the
# averaged tree probability for the winning class, so 1/n_classes at
# worst, 1.0 when every tree agrees), drawn as the fill's opacity. It
# shows where the trees DISAGREE -- on the example, 86% of the cells
# under UNCERTAIN_BELOW sat on a border between classes (measured
# live). It is not a distance-from-data measure: the farthest quarter
# of cells averaged 73% against 79% for the nearest, because a forest
# extends the nearest class outward with full conviction. The closing
# note below says so rather than letting the shading imply it.
confidence = model.predict_proba(centers).max(axis=1)
UNCERTAIN_BELOW = 0.6

half = cell_size / 2
cells = [
    Polygon([
        (cx - half, cy - half), (cx + half, cy - half),
        (cx + half, cy + half), (cx - half, cy + half),
        (cx - half, cy - half)
    ])
    for cx, cy in centers
]
grid_gdf = gpd.GeoDataFrame(
    {"predictedClass": predicted, "confidence": np.round(confidence, 2)}, geometry=cells, crs=calc_epsg
)
grid_wgs84 = grid_gdf.to_crs("EPSG:4326")

# The held-out blocks as outlines, so blocks mode reads on the map as
# what it is: whole areas the model was scored in without having seen
# anything inside them. Every block of the held-out fold is drawn,
# including ones with no points, to show the pattern the folds follow.
held_out_blocks = []
if can_split and use_blocks:
    for bx in range(BLOCKS_PER_SIDE):
        for by in range(BLOCKS_PER_SIDE):
            if (bx + 2 * by) % N_FOLDS == test_fold:
                x0, y0 = bminx + bx * block_size, bminy + by * block_size
                held_out_blocks.append(box(x0, y0, x0 + block_size, y0 + block_size))
held_out_blocks_wgs84 = gpd.GeoDataFrame(
    {"fold": [int(test_fold) if test_fold is not None else 0] * len(held_out_blocks)},
    geometry=held_out_blocks, crs=calc_epsg
).to_crs("EPSG:4326")

training_wgs84 = labeled.copy()
training_wgs84 = training_wgs84.rename(columns={classColumn: "class"})

# Per-point held-out flag and prediction, so a click on a confusion
# matrix cell can resolve to the individual points behind that cell.
# Training points carry an empty prediction rather than their own
# class: they were never predicted, and filling in the true value would
# make them indistinguishable from correctly classified test points.
# test_idx indexes X/y, which cover only the points that survived
# finite_mask above -- training_wgs84 keeps every labeled point,
# including any that couldn't be projected. The positions have to be
# mapped back through finite_mask rather than used directly: with the
# built-in example the two happen to line up (nothing is excluded), so
# a direct index would look correct here and silently mark the wrong
# points on an upload that spans too wide an area.
finite_positions = np.flatnonzero(finite_mask)
held_out_flags = np.zeros(len(training_wgs84), dtype=bool)
predicted_labels = np.full(len(training_wgs84), "", dtype=object)
if y_pred_test is not None:
    original_positions = finite_positions[test_idx]
    held_out_flags[original_positions] = True
    predicted_labels[original_positions] = y_pred_test
training_wgs84["heldOut"] = held_out_flags
training_wgs84["predictedClass"] = predicted_labels

{
    "trainingFeatures": training_wgs84[["class", "heldOut", "predictedClass", "geometry"]].__geo_interface__,
    "gridFeatures": grid_wgs84.__geo_interface__,
    "heldOutBlockFeatures": held_out_blocks_wgs84.__geo_interface__,
    "originalCrsFeatures": export_crs(grid_wgs84).__geo_interface__,
    "summary": {
        # count/crs duplicate what inspect already reported -- kept
        # here too so the stat card can show the full picture (Points,
        # Original CRS, Calculation CRS, ...) from this one value,
        # since WebGeoDS.Dashboard's compute.stats only ever receives
        # the compute cell's own return, not inspect's.
        "count": int(len(gdf)),
        "crs": str(original_crs),
        "calculationCrs": calc_crs_label,
        "classColumn": classColumn,
        "classLabels": class_labels,
        # Per-class training-point counts -- already computed above
        # (used there to decide which classes can be held out for
        # testing), reused here for the class-distribution chart
        # instead of a second pass over the same data.
        "classCounts": class_counts,
        "classAccuracy": class_accuracy,
        "confusion": confusion,
        "labeledCount": int(len(labeled)),
        "excludedCount": excluded_count,
        "trainCount": int(len(X_train)),
        "testCount": int(len(X_test)) if X_test is not None else 0,
        "accuracy": accuracy,
        "holdout": "Spatial blocks" if use_blocks else "Random points",
        "heldOutBlockCount": len(held_out_blocks),
        "blocksPerSide": BLOCKS_PER_SIDE,
        "cvRandom": cv_random,
        "cvBlocks": cv_blocks,
        "distanceMap": distance_map,
        "distanceRandom": distance_random,
        "distanceBlocks": distance_blocks,
        "nTrees": int(nTrees),
        "gridResolution": int(gridResolution),
        "gridCellCount": int(len(cells)),
        "meanConfidence": float(confidence.mean()),
        "uncertainCellCount": int((confidence < UNCERTAIN_BELOW).sum()),
        "uncertainBelow": UNCERTAIN_BELOW
    }
}
```

```{.webgeods-python #spatial-classifier-export-shp-py}
# Only run on demand (see the Dashboard config's download.shapefile
# below), not on every Compute: re-exports grid_wgs84 (the
# just-computed classified grid, already available from
# spatial-classifier-compute-py above) reprojected back to the CRS the
# file was UPLOADED in, as an actual shapefile (geopandas.to_file()),
# zips the resulting .shp/.shx/.dbf/.prj/.cpg in memory, and returns
# it base64-encoded -- same pattern as geojson-shapefile-validator.qmd's
# geometry-export-shp-py.
import base64
import io
import os
import zipfile

export_crs(grid_wgs84).to_file("/tmp/webgeods_export.shp", driver="ESRI Shapefile")

buf = io.BytesIO()
with zipfile.ZipFile(buf, "w", zipfile.ZIP_DEFLATED) as z:
    for fname in sorted(os.listdir("/tmp")):
        if fname.startswith("webgeods_export."):
            with open(f"/tmp/{fname}", "rb") as f:
                z.writestr(fname.replace("webgeods_export", "result"), f.read())

base64.b64encode(buf.getvalue()).decode("ascii")
```

*First run loads the Python engine — expect about a minute. Instant
after that, and again each time you come back to this page.*

<div id="sc-dashboard"></div>

<!-- Page-local, not site-wide (see blog/_quarto.yml's own comment on
     this): vega*.min.js + vega-embed.min.js together are ~828KB,
     meaningfully more than d3.min.js's ~280KB, and only this one tool
     needs them so far. -->
<script src="/vega.min.js"></script>
<script src="/vega-lite.min.js"></script>
<script src="/vega-embed.min.js"></script>
<script src="/vega-chart.js"></script>

<script>
document.addEventListener("DOMContentLoaded", () => {

  // Set by compute.onResult below, read by the training layer's
  // onClick and by the table cross-link cell further down the page.
  // On `window`, not a local `let`: a later {ojs} cell (the table
  // cross-link) runs in its own module scope and can't see a plain
  // script-local variable from this one -- same reason Dashboard
  // instances themselves are reached via WebGeoDS.Dashboard.find()
  // rather than a shared variable.
  window.scClassChart = null;

  new WebGeoDS.Dashboard({
    tool: "spatial-classifier",
    mount: "#sc-dashboard",
    layout: { sidePanel: { id: "sc-chart", flex: "1 1 280px", minWidth: "260px" } },
    upload: { languages: ["python"], kind: "vector", label: "📁 Upload" },
    example: {
      cellId: "spatial-classifier-example-py",
      kind: "geojson",
      status: "✓ example data loaded — pick the class column and Compute below."
    },
    emptyStats: [
      ["Points", "—"],
      ["—", "Upload a point GeoJSON/Shapefile or load the example above"]
    ],
    inspect: {
      cellId: "spatial-classifier-inspect-py",
      layers: [
        // No paint override -- the default circle style (shared/map.js's
        // own default) is exactly right for "uploaded, not yet
        // classified". Class colors only appear once Compute has run.
        { source: "spatial-classifier-training-py", from: (v) => v.features, type: "circle", fit: true }
      ],
      stats: (v) => {
        const s = v.summary;
        if (!s) return [["Points", "—"], ["—", "Upload a point GeoJSON/Shapefile or load the example above"]];
        const rows = [
          ["Points", s.count.toLocaleString()],
          ["Original CRS", s.crs === "None" || !s.crs ? "Unknown" : s.crs]
        ];
        if (v.crsWarning) rows.push(["CRS warning", v.crsWarning]);
        return rows;
      }
    },
    compute: {
      cellId: "spatial-classifier-compute-py",
      label: "▶ Compute",
      busyLabel: "⌛ Training...",
      inputs: [
        { kind: "select", name: "classColumn", label: "Class column:",
          options: (v) => v.summary?.columns ?? [],
          default: (v) => v.summary?.columns?.includes("class") ? "class" : v.summary?.columns?.[0] },
        // Blocks first, and the default: it's the honest estimate for a
        // map (see the compute cell). Random points stays one click away
        // so the gap between the two is something to see, not take on
        // faith; the stat card reports both either way.
        { kind: "select", name: "holdout", label: "Held out:",
          options: () => ["Spatial blocks", "Random points"],
          default: () => "Spatial blocks" },
        { kind: "slider", name: "nTrees", label: "Trees", range: [10, 300], value: 100, step: 10 },
        { kind: "slider", name: "gridResolution", label: "Grid resolution", range: [10, 40], value: 20, step: 5 }
      ],
      layers: [
        // Grid first, training points second: points draw ON TOP of
        // the filled grid, same z-order the original hand-wired
        // version relied on (setGeoJSON call order == layer order).
        { source: "spatial-classifier-grid-py", from: (v) => v.gridFeatures, type: "fill",
          paint: (v) => ({
            ...WebGeoDS.matchPaint(v.summary.classLabels, "predictedClass", {
              palette: WebGeoDS.DEFAULT_PALETTE, fill: true, strokeWidth: 1.5
            }),
            // Opacity carries the forest's confidence (see the compute
            // cell): nearly transparent at the lowest possible value,
            // 1/n_classes (the trees split evenly), up to solid where
            // every tree agrees. Colour still says WHICH class; how
            // much of it shows says how far to trust it.
            "fill-opacity": [
              "interpolate", ["linear"], ["get", "confidence"],
              1 / v.summary.classLabels.length, 0.08,
              1, 0.6
            ]
          }) },
        // Held-out blocks (blocks mode only; an empty collection in
        // random mode), between the grid and the points so the dots
        // stay clickable on top.
        { source: "spatial-classifier-blocks-py", from: (v) => v.heldOutBlockFeatures, type: "line",
          paint: () => ({ "line-color": "#2a2117", "line-width": 2, "line-dasharray": [2, 1.5] }) },
        { source: "spatial-classifier-training-py", from: (v) => v.trainingFeatures, type: "circle",
          paint: (v) => ({
            ...WebGeoDS.matchPaint(v.summary.classLabels, "class", {
              palette: WebGeoDS.DEFAULT_PALETTE, strokeWidth: 1.5
            }),
            // Held-out (test) points get a thicker outline, ALWAYS --
            // not only once one is selected. Without this, nothing on
            // the map says which ~20% of the dots the confusion matrix
            // and "Test accuracy" above are even about, before or
            // after a click; heldOut is already on every feature (see
            // the compute cell above).
            "circle-stroke-width": ["case", ["==", ["get", "heldOut"], true], 3, 1.5]
          }),
          // Map -> chart half of the cross-link (chart -> map is the
          // chart's own onSelect below) -- declared right next to the
          // layer it belongs to, same convention network-from-lines.qmd
          // already established for its own map<->diagram link.
          onClick: (feature) => window.scClassChart?.setSelected(feature.properties.class) }
      ],
      stats: (v) => {
        const r = v.summary;
        const rows = [
          ["Points", r.count.toLocaleString()],
          ["Original CRS", r.crs === "None" || !r.crs ? "Unknown" : r.crs],
          ["Calculation CRS", r.calculationCrs],
          ["Class column", r.classColumn],
          ["Classes found", r.classLabels.join(", ")],
          ["Labeled points", r.labeledCount.toLocaleString()]
        ];
        if (r.excludedCount > 0) {
          rows.push(["Excluded from training", `${r.excludedCount} (too far from the calculation UTM zone to project)`]);
        }
        rows.push([
          "Held out",
          r.testCount === 0 ? "—"
            : r.holdout === "Spatial blocks"
              ? `${r.testCount} points in ${r.heldOutBlockCount} of ${r.blocksPerSide * r.blocksPerSide} blocks (dashed on the map)`
              : `${r.testCount} random points`
        ]);
        rows.push(["Train / test split", r.testCount > 0 ? `${r.trainCount} / ${r.testCount}` : `${r.trainCount} / — (too few points to hold out)`]);
        // Python's None crosses over as JS `undefined`, not `null` (a
        // known site-wide ambiguity) -- loose equality catches both.
        rows.push(["Test accuracy", r.accuracy == null ? "N/A" : `${(r.accuracy * 100).toFixed(1)}%`]);
        const pct = (x) => x == null ? "N/A" : `${(x * 100).toFixed(0)}%`;
        rows.push(["5-fold CV accuracy", `random points ${pct(r.cvRandom)} · spatial blocks ${pct(r.cvBlocks)}`]);
        const metres = (x) => x == null ? "N/A" : `${Math.round(x).toLocaleString()} m`;
        rows.push([
          "Distance to nearest sample",
          `map cells ${metres(r.distanceMap)} · random test ${metres(r.distanceRandom)} · block test ${metres(r.distanceBlocks)} (medians)`
        ]);
        rows.push(["Trees", r.nTrees]);
        rows.push(["Grid cells", r.gridCellCount.toLocaleString()]);
        rows.push(["Mean confidence", `${(r.meanConfidence * 100).toFixed(0)}%`]);
        rows.push([
          "Uncertain cells",
          `${r.uncertainCellCount.toLocaleString()} (${(r.uncertainCellCount / r.gridCellCount * 100).toFixed(0)}%) under ${(r.uncertainBelow * 100).toFixed(0)}% agreement`
        ]);
        return rows;
      },
      legend: (v) => [
        ...v.summary.classLabels.map((label, i) => ({
          color: WebGeoDS.DEFAULT_PALETTE[i % WebGeoDS.DEFAULT_PALETTE.length],
          label
        })),
        // Documents the outline added to the training-points layer
        // above -- a style distinction, not a class, hence outline:
        // true (a hollow swatch) instead of one more filled color.
        { color: "#2a2117", label: "held out for testing", outline: true },
        ...(v.summary.heldOutBlockCount > 0 ? [{ color: "#2a2117", label: "held-out block (dashed)", outline: true }] : [])
      ],
      // Declarative table (compute.table -- Dashboard's first use of
      // it, replacing what used to be a hand-wired tableCell() OJS
      // cell below): the training points, cross-linked to the chart
      // via dashboard.table below and to the map by the training
      // layer's own onClick above. The grid/classification-areas
      // table further down this page stays hand-wired -- it has no
      // cross-link role of its own, and compute.table (v1) covers
      // one table per tool, the same "wait for a second real need"
      // discipline this project already applies elsewhere.
      table: {
        sources: ["spatial-classifier-training-py"],
        id: "sc-training-table",
        emptyMessage: "No results yet"
      },
      download: {
        getFeatures: (v) => v.originalCrsFeatures,
        filenameSuffix: "-classified-surface.geojson",
        defaultFilename: "classified-surface.geojson",
        shapefile: {
          cellId: "spatial-classifier-export-shp-py",
          filenameSuffix: "-classified-surface.zip",
          defaultFilename: "classified-surface-shapefile.zip"
        }
      },
      // Two class-distribution charts, stacked via Vega-Lite's own
      // `vconcat` inside ONE spec -- how many training points support
      // each class, and how accurate the model is on each class's
      // held-out points -- both pure functions of the compute value,
      // same as layers/stats/legend above, but rendered via onResult
      // rather than a declarative Dashboard field of its own (see
      // Dashboard's own doc comment on compute.diagram for why
      // onResult, not a second field, covers this). A single spec
      // (not two separate renderVegaChart() calls bridged by JS) means
      // Vega-Lite's own dataflow keeps the two panels in sync with no
      // custom code for that part -- only the cross-link OUT to map/
      // table (identical either way) is this file's job. BOTH panels
      // are independently clickable: shared/vega-chart.js's
      // selectParams accepts one point-selection param per view, all
      // funneled into the same shared classExternal/onSelect below.
      onResult: async (v) => {

        const dashboard =
          WebGeoDS.Dashboard.find("spatial-classifier");

        // Fades the training points so a matrix selection (always a
        // held-out subset, ~20% of the dots) doesn't have to compete
        // visually with the other 80% that were never part of the
        // evaluation. Left OFF for a bars selection, which selects
        // every point of a class -- training included -- so fading
        // them there would hide part of what that selection means.
        // setPaintProperty(), not a declarative layers[].paint field:
        // this reacts to a chart click, which the Dashboard config
        // has no hook for (paint is only ever recomputed from the
        // compute value, see the config's own layers[] doc comment).
        const setTrainingFade = (faded) => {
          const rawMap = dashboard.map?.map;
          if (!rawMap || !rawMap.getLayer("spatial-classifier-training-py")) {
            return;
          }
          rawMap.setPaintProperty(
            "spatial-classifier-training-py",
            "circle-opacity",
            faded ? ["case", ["==", ["get", "heldOut"], true], 1, 0.12] : 1
          );
        };

        // The selection highlight is a SEPARATE overlay layer drawn ON
        // TOP of the training layer (see shared/map-table.js's own
        // selectionPaint()), with a flat color+radius and no stroke --
        // so a selected held-out point loses its thicker ring the
        // moment it's selected: the opaque highlight circle covers the
        // base point, ring included. Called after EVERY selectMany()
        // below, not just once: that same source gets its paint
        // reset to the flat default on every single selection change
        // (setGeoJSON() re-applies options.paint each time), which
        // would otherwise wipe this override out on the very next
        // click.
        const restyleHighlightStroke = () => {
          const rawMap = dashboard.map?.map;
          if (!rawMap) {
            return;
          }
          // No public API exposes the overlay's own layer id --
          // map-table.js deliberately keeps SELECTION_SOURCE_ID
          // internal, one per call to _tableController() (see its own
          // doc comment: "per-CALL, not a fixed name"). Found instead
          // by its "__webgeods_selection_" prefix, stable even though
          // the numeric suffix isn't -- exactly one such layer can
          // exist here, since this tool has only one compute.table.
          const highlightLayer =
            rawMap.getStyle().layers.find((l) => l.id.startsWith("__webgeods_selection_"));
          if (!highlightLayer) {
            // Nothing selected right now -- removeGeoJSON() already
            // tore the layer down (selectByKeys()'s own doc comment).
            return;
          }
          rawMap.setPaintProperty(highlightLayer.id, "circle-stroke-color", "#2a2117");
          rawMap.setPaintProperty(
            highlightLayer.id,
            "circle-stroke-width",
            ["case", ["==", ["get", "heldOut"], true], 3, 0]
          );
        };

        window.scClassChart?.destroy();
        window.scClassChart = null;

        if (!v) {
          // Called with null on reset -- nothing to draw. The layer
          // itself is gone too (Reset clears the map's own sources),
          // but the paint override isn't tied to the data, so it would
          // otherwise carry over, faded, into the next Compute run.
          setTrainingFade(false);
          return;
        }

        // Every row of both panels carries its selection key under the
        // SAME field name, `key`: shared/vega-chart.js reads one
        // keyField for the whole spec (see its selectParams doc
        // comment), so two panels keying on differently-named fields
        // would leave one of them returning undefined on click. The
        // distribution panel's key is the class; the matrix's is the
        // "true>predicted" pair, and onSelect below tells them apart by
        // the separator.
        const PAIR_SEPARATOR = ">";

        const distRows =
          Object.entries(v.summary.classCounts).map(([cls, count]) => ({ cls, count, key: cls }));

        // Classes with NO held-out points (a singleton class, or no
        // test split at all -- see class_accuracy's own doc comment in
        // the compute cell above) are simply absent here, not shown at
        // 0% -- an untested class isn't the same claim as "always
        // wrong".
        const accRows =
          Object.entries(v.summary.classAccuracy)
            .map(([cls, a]) => ({ cls, accuracy: a.accuracy, testCount: a.testCount, key: cls }));

        const confusionRows =
          (v.summary.confusion ?? []).map((c) => ({
            trueClass: c.trueClass,
            predictedClass: c.predictedClass,
            count: c.count,
            correct: c.trueClass === c.predictedClass,
            key: `${c.trueClass}${PAIR_SEPARATOR}${c.predictedClass}`
          }));

        // A confusion matrix is only readable while it stays small: the
        // class column comes from an uploaded file and can hold dozens
        // of values, and a 30x30 grid of rects in a narrow side panel
        // tells nobody anything. Past that, the per-class accuracy bars
        // are kept instead -- they degrade into a long readable list
        // where a matrix degrades into confetti.
        const MAX_MATRIX_CLASSES = 6;
        const useMatrix =
          confusionRows.length > 0 && v.summary.classLabels.length <= MAX_MATRIX_CLASSES;

        // Shared color scale/condition, used identically by both
        // panels below -- written once rather than duplicated, so the
        // two can't silently drift apart.
        const classColor = {
          "condition": { "test": "datum.cls === classExternal", "value": "#ffeb3b" },
          "field": "cls",
          "type": "nominal",
          "scale": { "domain": v.summary.classLabels, "range": WebGeoDS.DEFAULT_PALETTE },
          "legend": null
        };

        window.scClassChart = await WebGeoDS.renderVegaChart(dashboard.sidePanelEl, {
          "$schema": "https://vega.github.io/schema/vega-lite/v5.json",
          // "fit-x", not the single-view chart's own "fit": each
          // panel below sets its OWN fixed "height" (130/100), only
          // "width": "container" needs to actually fit the available
          // box -- omitting this entirely (as this spec originally
          // did, carried over from before the vconcat rewrite) left
          // Vega-Lite's own default autosize in charge, which computed
          // a width wider than sidePanelEl's real box for a
          // concatenated view -- confirmed live (a chart visibly
          // clipped on its right edge by sidePanelEl's own
          // overflow:hidden, not a rendering glitch).
          "autosize": { "type": "fit-x", "contains": "padding" },
          // Shared across BOTH panels below -- declared at THIS level
          // (not inside either panel's own spec), the same reasoning
          // shared/vega-chart.js's own doc comment gives for a
          // multi-view spec. Each panel's OWN "params" entry (its
          // point-selection) stays scoped to that panel alone.
          "params": [
            { "name": "classExternal", "value": null }
          ],
          "vconcat": [
            {
              // Not "Training points": classCounts is taken over ALL
              // labeled points, before the train/test split (see the
              // compute cell above), and a click here selects every
              // point of a class regardless of heldOut -- training
              // AND test together.
              "title": "Labeled points per class",
              "width": "container",
              "height": 130,
              "data": { "values": distRows },
              // Vega-Lite's own default clear trigger (dblclick) is
              // kept as-is: tried overriding it to "click" for a more
              // intuitive single-click-to-deselect, found LIVE (via
              // Playwright, not just reasoning) that it also
              // intercepts the SAME click that selects a bar in the
              // first place -- one physical click firing both
              // "select" and "clear" raced and silently cancelled the
              // selection. Reverted rather than risk the real,
              // reported bug (chart -> map/table not propagating) for
              // a minor, unreported UX polish item.
              "params": [
                { "name": "classSelectDist", "select": { "type": "point", "fields": ["key"] } }
              ],
              "mark": "bar",
              "encoding": {
                "x": { "field": "cls", "type": "nominal", "title": "Class" },
                "y": { "field": "count", "type": "quantitative", "title": "Labeled points" },
                // Selected -> the same yellow shared/map.js's own
                // highlight() uses (--dataviz-selection), so a
                // selection looks the same regardless of which view
                // (map, either chart panel) it started from.
                "color": classColor
              }
            },
            useMatrix ? {
              "title": { "text": "Confusion matrix", "subtitle": "held-out points only" },
              "width": "container",
              "height": 130,
              "data": { "values": confusionRows },
              "layer": [
                {
                  // The selection param belongs to THIS layer, not to
                  // the layered spec around it: declared one level up,
                  // Vega-Lite pushes it into every child and the rect
                  // and text layers then register the same signal
                  // twice, which fails outright with "Duplicate signal
                  // name: classSelectAcc_tuple" and leaves the whole
                  // chart undrawn.
                  "params": [
                    { "name": "classSelectAcc", "select": { "type": "point", "fields": ["key"] } }
                  ],
                  "mark": { "type": "rect", "stroke": "#ffffff", "strokeWidth": 1 },
                  "encoding": {
                    "color": {
                      // Selected cell takes the same yellow a map or
                      // table selection uses; otherwise correct cells
                      // (the diagonal) are green and errors red, so the
                      // shape of the mistakes reads before any number
                      // does. Opacity carries the count.
                      "condition": { "test": "datum.key === classExternal", "value": "#ffeb3b" },
                      "field": "correct",
                      "type": "nominal",
                      "scale": { "domain": [true, false], "range": ["#42583c", "#ab502b"] },
                      "legend": null
                    },
                    "opacity": {
                      "field": "count", "type": "quantitative",
                      "scale": { "range": [0.35, 1] }, "legend": null
                    }
                  }
                },
                {
                  // The count written into the cell: colour alone reads
                  // poorly as a magnitude, and with a handful of
                  // classes there is room for the number itself.
                  "mark": { "type": "text", "fontSize": 11, "fontWeight": 600 },
                  "encoding": {
                    "text": { "field": "count", "type": "quantitative" },
                    "color": { "value": "#ffffff" }
                  }
                }
              ],
              "encoding": {
                "x": { "field": "predictedClass", "type": "nominal", "title": "Predicted",
                       "scale": { "domain": v.summary.classLabels } },
                "y": { "field": "trueClass", "type": "nominal", "title": "Actual",
                       "scale": { "domain": v.summary.classLabels } }
              }
            } : {
              "title": { "text": "Test accuracy per class", "subtitle": "held-out points only" },
              "width": "container",
              "height": 100,
              "data": { "values": accRows },
              "params": [
                { "name": "classSelectAcc", "select": { "type": "point", "fields": ["key"] } }
              ],
              "mark": "bar",
              "encoding": {
                "x": { "field": "cls", "type": "nominal", "title": "Class" },
                "y": { "field": "accuracy", "type": "quantitative", "title": "Test accuracy",
                       "scale": { "domain": [0, 1] }, "axis": { "format": "%" } },
                "color": classColor
              }
            }
          ]
        }, {
          selectParams: ["classSelectDist", "classSelectAcc"],
          externalParam: "classExternal",
          keyField: "key",
          // Chart -> map+table half of the cross-link. Reuses the
          // SAME selection mechanism a map click or a table-row click
          // already drives -- reached directly as `dashboard.table`
          // now that the table is compute.table (Dashboard's own
          // declarative field, see the config above), not a
          // WebGeoDS.Map.findTableSelection(id) lookup as it was
          // before that field existed -- instead of shared/map.js's
          // separate highlight() helper: highlight() only touches the
          // map, leaving the table's own row styling out of sync, AND
          // (found live, while testing this) its featureIds filter
          // silently matched nothing: v.trainingFeatures.features[].id
          // comes through as a STRING (geopandas's own
          // __geo_interface__ -> JSON -> JS bridge), but MapLibre's
          // actual rendered feature ids are numbers, so a
          // string/number-mismatched filter matched zero features.
          // Routing through selectMany() -- built FOR real MapLibre
          // ids -- sidesteps that whole class of bug and keeps
          // map+table in sync in one call, selecting EVERY point of
          // the clicked class (a real, reported requirement: a class
          // is many points, not one representative one -- unlike
          // network-from-lines.qmd's node/diagram cross-link, where a
          // click really is a single node).
          onSelect: async (selectedKey) => {

            const tableSelection =
              dashboard.table;

            if (!tableSelection) {
              return;
            }

            if (!selectedKey) {
              // Deselected -- also drops the training-point fade, so
              // leaving either panel this way always returns the map
              // to its normal state.
              setTrainingFade(false);
              // Bar deselected -- selectMany() toggles OFF when
              // called with the SAME set again, same as re-clicking
              // every one of those features/rows by hand.
              if (window.scLastTableKeys) {
                await tableSelection.selectMany(window.scLastTableKeys);
                restyleHighlightStroke();
              }
              window.scLastTableKeys = null;
              return;
            }

            // Two shapes of key arrive here, told apart by the
            // separator (see PAIR_SEPARATOR above). A class on its own
            // comes from the distribution panel and means every point
            // of that class. A "true>predicted" pair comes from the
            // confusion matrix and means only the HELD-OUT points
            // behind that cell -- so clicking an off-diagonal cell puts
            // exactly the misclassified points on the map, which is the
            // question a confusion matrix is usually asked.
            const [trueClass, predictedClass] =
              selectedKey.split(PAIR_SEPARATOR);

            // Set before the keys lookup below (not after), so it
            // still applies even in the rare case a cell or class
            // resolves to zero points.
            setTrainingFade(predictedClass !== undefined);

            const matches =
              predictedClass === undefined
                ? (p) => p.class === trueClass
                : (p) => p.heldOut === true && p.class === trueClass && p.predictedClass === predictedClass;

            const keys =
              v.trainingFeatures.features
                .filter((f) => matches(f.properties))
                .map((f) => `spatial-classifier-training-py:${Number(f.id)}`);

            if (keys.length === 0) {
              return;
            }

            window.scLastTableKeys =
              keys;

            await tableSelection.selectMany(keys);
            restyleHighlightStroke();

          }
        });

      }
    }
  });

});
</script>

<div class="webgeods-closing-note" style="margin-top: 4px;">
The filled grid is the model's prediction; the dots on top are your
own labeled points, colored the same way. How solid a cell looks is
how much of the forest agrees on its class: solid where nearly every
tree votes the same way, faded where they split. On the example, most
faded cells sit on the borders between classes, where nearby samples
disagree. What the shading can't flag is distance: a forest can be
just as confident far from every sample, simply carrying the nearest
class outward, so a solid patch with no dots in it is still a guess.
"Uncertain cells" above counts the ones where fewer than 60% of the
trees agree.
<br><br>
By default the test points are whole <strong>blocks</strong> of the map
(dashed), not points scattered at random. Scattered test points
flatter a map: their neighbours usually stay in training, so the model
can copy the point next door instead of predicting somewhere new. The
"5-fold CV accuracy" row scores both ways, every point tested once: on
the built-in example, random points score about 76% and spatial
blocks about 57%.
<br><br>
Which one describes the map? The row below it answers that: a score
only holds for predictions made about as far from the data as its
test points were. On the example, random test points sit 27 m from
the nearest training point (a site-mate), the map's cells about 73 m,
and block test points 193 m. So the random score flatters the map and
the blocks score is on the cautious side, but closer: blocks sized to
match the map's distances score about 61-65%. On your own
file, if the block distance is far above the map's, the blocks score
is pessimistic; if it's close, it's about right.
<br><br>
The map itself is drawn from a forest trained on every point; the
held-out points are left out only of the separate forest that scores
it. The thicker-outlined dots are those held-out ones (see the
legend), and their predictions in the table and the matrix below come
from that scoring forest, the one that never saw them. A dot of a
different color from the cell under it is a point the map gets wrong
even though it was trained on it.
<br><br>
The matrix reads actual class down the side, predicted class across
the bottom, so the diagonal is what the model got right and everything
off it is where the mistakes went. Click any cell to put those points
on the map and the table: unlike the bar chart above it, which selects
every point of a class, a cell selects only the <em>held-out</em>
points behind that cell (the same thicker-outlined dots) — an
off-diagonal click is therefore the shortest way to see exactly which
points were misclassified, and
where they are.
</div>

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
//| output: false
// A top-level OJS cell can run BEFORE DOMContentLoaded (Quarto's OJS
// runtime is a deferred module, but not deferred THAT much) -- the
// same race WebGeoDS.Dashboard's own doc comment explains for why it
// mounts on DOMContentLoaded instead of as an {ojs} cell itself.
// Waiting it out here, once, is simpler than every consumer below
// re-deriving it.
classifierDashboard = {
  await new Promise((resolve) => {
    if (document.readyState !== "loading") { resolve(); return; }
    document.addEventListener("DOMContentLoaded", resolve, { once: true });
  });
  const dashboard = WebGeoDS.Dashboard.find("spatial-classifier");
  await dashboard.ready();
  return dashboard;
}
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
//| output: false
// The training-points table itself is now compute.table (see the
// Dashboard config above) -- dashboard.table is the SAME
// _tableController() handle a hand-wired tableCell() call would have
// returned, reached directly (no WebGeoDS.Map.findTableSelection(id)
// lookup needed) since classifierDashboard already holds it.
classifierTable = classifierDashboard.table.element
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
//| output: false
// Table -> chart half of the cross-link (map -> chart is the training
// layer's own onClick, chart -> map is the chart's own onSelect --
// both declared in the Dashboard config above). SELECTION_CHANGE_EVENT
// fires on a tableCell() call's own container from ANY cause (a row
// click, a map click, or the chart's own onSelect calling
// selectMany() for a whole class -- shared/map.js's own tableCell()
// doc comment) -- `e.detail.keys` is "sourceId:id" for every currently
// selected feature, so an id half maps straight back to a
// trainingFeatures entry via its own top-level `id`.
{
  classifierDashboard.table.element.addEventListener(WebGeoDS.Map.SELECTION_CHANGE_EVENT, (e) => {
    const keys = e.detail.keys;
    if (keys.length === 0) {
      window.scClassChart?.setSelected(null);
      return;
    }
    if (keys.length > 1) {
      // A whole-class selection reaches this listener too, but only
      // ever as an ECHO of the chart's own selectMany() call (a row/
      // map click always selects exactly one feature) -- the chart
      // already reflects it, so there's nothing to derive here.
      // Treating this as "no matching single feature" would be wrong
      // in the other direction: it would clear the chart's own bar
      // highlight right after the user's click set it.
      return;
    }
    const id = Number(keys[0].split(":")[1]);
    const value = classifierDashboard.value;
    // Number(f.id): trainingFeatures' own ids come through as STRINGS
    // (geopandas's __geo_interface__ -> JSON -> JS bridge) -- the same
    // string/number mismatch already found and fixed in the chart's
    // own onSelect above, reintroduced here independently and caught
    // by testing this direction specifically, not assumed fixed by
    // the other one.
    const feature = value?.trainingFeatures?.features?.find((f) => Number(f.id) === id);
    if (feature) window.scClassChart?.setSelected(feature.properties.class);
  });
}
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
//| output: false
// The grid cells the model predicted across the whole uploaded
// extent (predictedClass per cell) — the same features the download
// button exports (reprojected to the input's own CRS there; shown
// here in the working WGS84 the map itself uses).
classifierGridTable = classifierDashboard.map.tableCell(["spatial-classifier-grid-py"], null, Generators, {
  emptyMessage: "No results yet"
})
```
